paragraphs: Huddersfield is part of Kirklees, so children in care from the town are looked after by Kirklees Council's fostering service and by the independent agencies shown above. The council wants more carers who live in or near Kirklees, so that children can stay close to their friends, schools and families, and in April 2026 it said it would particularly like to hear from people who could care for older children or brothers and sisters. It welcomes people of all backgrounds and ages, and says that being single, your income or renting your home will not affect an application.

Kirklees says that going from a first enquiry to approval usually takes around five months, depending on your circumstances. The five steps are an enquiry and a chat with a fostering adviser, a phone call and home visit, training before approval (which a partner can join), an assessment with DBS and medical checks, and a fostering panel, which makes a recommendation to the person who takes the final decision.

Kirklees carers receive weekly payments and a skills payment set by the child's age and the carer's skill level, two weeks' extra pay towards a summer holiday, and extra payments for birthdays and for Christmas or religious festivals, as well as a fuel allowance and help with furniture and equipment. The council does not publish the amounts online and asks people to contact it for the latest figures. Support includes a supervising social worker, Mockingbird groups of foster families living near one another, regular support groups, free Fostering Network membership, 28 days of paid time off a year and out-of-hours help.
Speak to Kirklees and to two or three of the services above to compare the children they need homes for, their training and the support they offer.
